conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be helping take care of you during this hospital stay. Can you tell me what brought you in today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. I’ve been having worse pain in my upper belly again, going to my back. It started a few days ago and hasn’t let up. I’ve been nauseous and vomiting, so I stopped eating. I’ve been on TPN at home, but it’s not helping like it used to.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. This sounds like a flare of your chronic pancreatitis. We’ll keep you on bowel rest and continue your TPN for nutrition. We’ll also give you IV fluids and medications for pain and nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. The pain is constant and worse when I move. Staying still helps a little. I’ve had more bad days lately—maybe four or five a week now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s tough. We’ll monitor your symptoms closely. Your lipase was slightly elevated, but not extremely high, which fits with chronic rather than acute severe inflammation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m worried it might be something worse, like cancer. My mom died of pancreatic cancer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s an important concern, and I understand why you’re worried. To be safe, we’ve ordered an MRCP to get a detailed look at your pancreas and rule out any tumors or blockages.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I also noticed my PICC line wasn’t working as well. It felt like it was backing up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the chest X-ray showed your PICC line has shifted a bit—it’s now in the brachiocephalic vein instead of the SVC. It’s still usable for now, but we may need to replace it soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. I’ve been changing the dressing myself, so maybe that’s why.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That could be part of it. Because it’s been in so long and you’re doing the care at home, we recommend replacing it within the next few weeks—or sooner if you notice redness or swelling.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I’ll watch for that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How’s your pain today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still there, but maybe a little less intense. The nausea is better since the Zofran.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s good progress. We’ll keep you on IV anti-nausea meds and adjust your pain medication as needed. Your labs are stable—no signs of infection or kidney issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been feeling a bit down lately. This whole thing is exhausting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I hear you. Chronic illness takes a toll. You’re on sertraline and bupropion—we can talk to your psychiatrist about whether adjustments are needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Maybe. I just feel stuck sometimes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The MRCP is scheduled for tomorrow. It will help us see if there’s any blockage or pseudocyst. So far, no signs of cancer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. What does the test involve?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s an MRI with a special contrast and a hormone called secretin to stimulate your pancreas. It’s non-invasive and will give us detailed images.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’m ready for anything that helps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did great on the MRCP. The results are back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news. No tumors or pseudocysts. The pancreas shows changes from chronic pancreatitis, but the response to secretin was nearly normal—no blockage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s such a relief. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also saw stable liver hemangiomas and a small kidney cyst—nothing concerning. So we’ll keep focusing on managing your symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning to replace your PICC line tomorrow. It’s safer to have it properly placed, especially since you’re on long-term TPN.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it a big procedure?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, it’s done with ultrasound and fluoroscopy. Local anesthesia, and you’ll be awake. A new line will be placed in the same arm, and the old one removed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I trust you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The PICC replacement went smoothly. New line is in the SVC, working well. You can resume TPN through it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t feel much. Just some pressure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s normal. We’ll keep monitoring the site. Remember to watch for redness or drainage and let us know.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your pain and nausea are improving. We’re going to try switching you to oral hydromorphone and Phenergan suppositories.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oral meds? I haven’t kept anything down in days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start low and slow. The Phenergan suppository can help if you can’t keep pills down. It’s more sedating, so be careful with pain meds together.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll be careful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We’re planning to start advancing your diet—maybe clear liquids tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. I miss drinking water without worrying.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You tolerated the clear liquids well. We’ll move to full liquids today—broth, juice, maybe some yogurt.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I had some apple juice this morning and felt okay. No nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. We’ll keep monitoring, but this is a good sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re thinking about discharge in the next day or two. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Much better. Still some dull pain, but manageable. I’m ready to go home, but nervous about it flaring again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Totally understandable. You’ll continue TPN at home and have visiting nurse support. We’re also sending you home with saline bags for dehydration if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That helps. What about my meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re stopping gabapentin—it doesn’t seem to be helping your pain. You’ll keep your fentanyl patch, omeprazole, and the new Phenergan for nausea as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I did feel a bit foggy on the gabapentin. Maybe it’s for the best.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re finalizing your discharge plan. You’ll go home tomorrow morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. Will I need to come back for follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’ll see your gastroenterologist in a week. They’ll review your MRCP and adjust long-term management. Also, please get weekly labs and fax them in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll make sure to do that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And remember—watch the PICC site. If it gets red or painful, call your team. They may want to resite it in the next few weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re cleared to go home. I’ll go over your discharge instructions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’m ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue TPN as before. Use saline infusions if you can’t keep fluids down. Take your meds as prescribed, especially the new Phenergan for nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And stop the gabapentin, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, discontinue it. If pain worsens, use the hydromorphone sparingly and call your GI doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I’ll take it slow at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve made great progress. We’re confident you can manage this at home with support. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I really appreciate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The visiting nurse will check in tomorrow. Call us if anything changes before then.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Have a safe trip home.
